summary: Intro demo of Redwood model catalog decision matrix tailored to Cascade AI. Walked through open-model selection, benchmark interpretation, and compatibility mapping to kernels/hardware. Discussed cost/latency tradeoffs, routing policies, and security considerations (VPC, KMS, SOC2). Agreed to send security docs and a pilot plan.
meeting_header: Date: 2026-09-02 | Start: 14:00 PDT | Duration: 52m | Redwood: Jordan Lee, Priya Nair, Tom Alvarez | Cascade AI: Maya Chen, Luis Ortega, Nina Park, Owen Blake
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Jordan from Redwood, i think priya and tom are on with me, uh we scheduled 50 minutes to walk through the catalog decision matrix and a few benches, make sure it maps to your platform. quick intro?
[00:14] Maya Chen: Thanks Jordan, Maya here — we run model selection for internal apps at Cascade, main goal today is understanding tradeoffs for open models and how we pick for low-latency API usage.
[00:27] Priya Nair: Hi Maya, Luis, Nina — i'm Priya, i'm the solutions engineer. quick agenda: 1) catalog demo — filters, compatibility matrix, and scoring; 2) bench interpretation — we've got latency/cost per token and accuracy deltas; 3) routing/fallbacks and private options. Sound good?
[00:44] Luis Ortega: Yup, that's perfect. we have an existing self-hosted option but we hit perf cliffs at scale, and we'd like to understand dedicated vs hosted for steady 8–12k RPS peaks.
[00:58] Jordan Lee: Great, we'll surface the routing policies that help with exactly that. ok jumping into the console — 
[01:12] [screen share noise]
[01:20] Priya Nair: This is the model catalog view. Note the top-left filters: task, sequence length, preferred hardware, and compatibility tier. you can also add a custom bench column — we uploaded your quick test prompts earlier and i pinned them.
[01:38] Nina Park: I see a "compat score" column — how is that computed?
[01:42] Priya Nair: Good question -- compat score is a heuristic combining kernel mapping compatibility, quantization friendliness, and historical bench variance. It's weighted — default is 40% bench latency, 35% kernel match, 25% memory/quantization risk. You can tune weights.
[02:00] Maya Chen: When you say kernel match, do you mean the runtime chooses specific CUDA/cuBLAS kernels? We run on a mix of A100/NVIDIA and some on Ampere-like.
[02:12] Priya Nair: Yeah, kernel mapping refers to the runtime's kernel selection for attention and matmul paths; for example some LLaMA variants map better to our fused attention kernels. We also include a note if a model needs custom fused ops or if it prefers memory-efficient kernels.
[02:28] Tom Alvarez: small aside: sometimes the transcript will show "K V cash" — but it's KV cache (laughs).
[02:33] Maya Chen: (laughs) we saw that in your docs.
[02:38] [00:03:10] Jordan Lee: moving on — here's a compatibility matrix view where rows are models and columns are hardware lanes + quant profiles. green means we've validated on that lane; amber is 'works but with caveats' and red is 'not recommended'
[03:00] Luis Ortega: Can you demo how we'd pick a model for 256 token avg seq with strict 120ms p95?
[03:10] Priya Nair: Sure. Filter by avg seq 200-300, target p95 <120ms and set routing preference to 'latency-first'. see these top two picks — open-variant-7B-quant and f7b-int8. open-variant-7B-quant shows p95 ~95ms on A100 with batching 4, but cost per 1k tokens is higher because we couldn't squeeze the KV cache as aggressively.
[03:36] Maya Chen: The cost delta — can you show numbers? our rough budget is $1200/month for prod for that endpoint.
[03:44] Priya Nair: Right — on hosted API that equates roughly to X tokens — (notes) — For our estimate, open-variant-7B-quant is approximately $0.28 per 1k tokens; f7b-int8 is $0.18 per 1k tokens but p95 is 140ms unless pinned to dedicated capacity. We'll attach a spreadsheet with the math.
[04:05] Maya Chen: Okay, so dedicated would pull the p95 down?
[04:10] Jordan Lee: Usually yes — Dedicated gives better isolation and predictable batching which helps p95s. Our Dedicated offering also supports autoscale with burst lanes. there are tradeoffs on commit costs.
[04:22] Nina Park: Any difference in metrics retention, audit logs, or encryption between hosted and private?
[04:29] Tom Alvarez: By default hosted has standard retention and audit logs in console; Private (VPC) gives you customer-managed KMS/HSM and we can route logs to your CloudWatch/Splunk; we also have SOC2 artifacts which we'll share.
[04:42] [04:55] Luis Ortega: Do you support bring-your-own-model (BYOM) in the catalog? we have some tuned forks.
[04:59] Priya Nair: Yes, BYOM is supported in Private and Dedicated. In the catalog you can upload a model artifact or point to a registry; we run an automated compatibility check that outputs a 'lift' score and kernel mapping suggestions. For some forks we run a lightweight compile step and report expected quant performance.
[05:18] Maya Chen: I want to dig into the benchmark interpretation bit — we sometimes see accuracy regressions after quant. how do you present that?
[05:26] Priya Nair: We present bench decks with signal columns: baseline unquantized accuracy, quantized delta, generation quality metrics, and a prompt-level diff. There is also a quality-monitoring hook you can install to track regression alerts on your evaluation set.
[05:40] Owen Blake: from procurement perspective: what's required to start a pilot timeline wise?
[05:46] Jordan Lee: usually 2–4 weeks. week 0: onboarding and infra kickoff; week 1: short pilot with 100k tokens/day to validate latency and routing; week 2–3: iterate on quant/profile and rollout canary. we'll send a sample SOW.
[06:03] Maya Chen: Are there any gotchas with tokenization differences between models? our prompt templates assume GPT-like bytepair tokens.
[06:11] Priya Nair: Yes tokenization differences are in the compatibility matrix. we surface tokenization family and estimated token delta for your corpus so you can model cost impact. sometimes we recommend re-tokenizing or minimal prompt changes.
[06:25] [06:30] Jordan Lee: quick pivot to the decision matrix — here you can weigh accuracy, latency, and cost and the table re-sorts. i'll manually bump latency weight up to 50% — notice the top candidate switches.
[06:43] Maya Chen: that's helpful. can we export the shortlist to CSV with bench trace?
[06:48] Priya Nair: yes there's an export button. i'll export and share the link after the call.
[06:55] Luis Ortega: you mentioned routing policies — can those be per-customer or per-token-route?
[07:02] Priya Nair: per-route. routing is part of the API config. you can route by priority: latency, cost, or region; there are fallbacks — e.g., if dedicated lane is full, fallback to a cheaper variant with a small delay. you can also pin key routes to dedicated pools.
[07:20] Nina Park: do you support prefix caching for chat use-cases?
[07:24] Tom Alvarez: yes we support prefix/KV caching; for chat we materialize KV caches per conversation, and caching significantly reduces token compute on repeated contexts. also note that longer contexts can change kernel selection.
[07:37] [07:45] Maya Chen: security quick question — KMS integration for private, do you support AWS KMS and GCP KMS?
[07:53] Tom Alvarez: yes both and HSM on-prem. for hosted we manage keys unless you select Private with customer-managed keys.
[07:59] Owen Blake: any enterprise customers using private for regulated data?
[08:03] Jordan Lee: Yes, several finance and health customers. We can share redacted references.
[08:10] [08:30] Priya Nair: Ok flipping back to bench interpretation: here's a sample run showing p50/p95 and tokenized cost. the sheet also includes a 'stability' column that shows variance across 10 runs — helps spot flaky models.
[08:44] Maya Chen: Interesting — how often do you re-run benches?
[08:48] Priya Nair: We re-run nightly for our catalog and on-demand for customer uploads. We also run a regression alert if a model's perf drifts >10% p95.
[08:58] Luis Ortega: there's a mention of "quant profiles" — do you provide automated suggestions or is it manual?
[09:03] Priya Nair: We provide automated suggestions — Optimize will recommend INT8, 4-bit modes, or mixed precision with expected perf and quality impact. you can preview the expected accuracy delta before applying.
[09:16] Maya Chen: Could you give a concrete example where int8 caused a 2–3% drop on NER tasks?
[09:22] Priya Nair: Sure — in the bench notes, open-variant-13B-int8 showed a 2.7% F1 drop on our NER eval; we then suggested 4-bit QAT for that model which recovered most of the loss at slightly higher cost.
[09:36] [09:50] Nina Park: Are there guardrails for hallucinations or safety filters?
[09:54] Tom Alvarez: There are post-filter hooks and rerankers; you can plug in a reranking microservice or use Redwood's built-in safety filters with custom rules. That is part of the pipeline we recommend for production.
[10:08] Maya Chen: Ok. any late-stage concerns from our side — latency vs cost tradeoffs is the big one. Also procurement needs the SSO/SAML and SOC2 doc.
[10:19] Jordan Lee: We'll share SOC2 and SAML details — Priya will package the deck and spreadsheets.
[10:25] Owen Blake: Also send a short note on data residency — we need EU region confirmation for some customers.
[10:31] Priya Nair: Noted. We support region routing and can pin an instance to EU region, we'll confirm available regions for Private.
[10:40] [11:05] Jordan Lee: Two quick feature notes: 1) the "catalog picklist" API allows programmatic shortlist selection; 2) Optimize can autosuggest batching knobs per route. Both useful for automation.
[11:18] Luis Ortega: Programmatic shortlist is key for automation. can we call it from our CI to run regression tests?
[11:24] Priya Nair: Yes, you can trigger bench runs via API and fetch results — many customers integrate with CI.
[11:32] Maya Chen: sweet. let's talk timeline — assuming we get the docs next week, can pilot start the week of Sept 14?
[11:39] Jordan Lee: That seems doable. We'll send SOW and pilot checklist today/tomorrow.
[11:45] [12:00] Priya Nair: i'll also include a short runbook for quick private deployment steps and a sample prompt set template.
[12:06] Maya Chen: Thanks Priya.
[12:09] Jordan Lee: okay last thing, any competitors you want us to call out in the follow-up?
[12:14] Maya Chen: They asked about Anthropic and a few teams using OpenAI endpoints and internal self-host.
[12:20] Jordan Lee: Great, we'll include a short comparison. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the export and security docs.
[12:30] [End 00:52:00]
